fact_text: Fair value of a listed IPP has two parts: government arrears it is owed, adjusted for the likely settlement, plus the value of future earnings from its remaining plant economics; compare that with market value.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In a negotiated settlement an IPP may lose the late-payment surcharge, so cash collected can land about 15-25% below the book amount of arrears.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cash received from government arrears is typically used first to repay bank debt, so the amount left for dividends is smaller than the receipt; dividends should not be assumed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The government lowers per-unit power cost through three levers: cancelling IPP contracts, converting capacity-payment plants to pay-per-unit, and rescheduling debt-related payments of remaining IPPs.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Once an IPP's contract is cancelled or renegotiated, the fixed capacity payments for its remaining contract years can disappear, cutting future earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Disputed taxes an IPP has already paid can be made refundable by the government in a settlement if the cases go against the company, shifting that downside to the state.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Owners may keep an IPP plant and convert it to cheaper coal fuel rather than scrap it, since a converted plant can sell power to private customers under the planned market structure.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Under pay-per-unit contracts the buyer dispatches the cheapest-to-run plants first, so a plant with a low variable fuel cost gets more units and higher profit per unit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Per unit of power, furnace-oil plants cost the most to run, LNG plants come next, and plants on local gas are the cheapest.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A 200 MW plant running at a 70% load factor through the year produces roughly one billion units of electricity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The planned competitive trading bilateral contract market (CTBCM) would let power plants sell electricity directly to private customers instead of only to the state buyer.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Furnace-oil IPPs have weak fuel-cost economics, so their future earnings are hard to rely on; valuation should lean on receivables and cash rather than on those earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'What is happening in Power Sector - Everything you need to know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Nishat Chunian Power is one of the roughly 200 MW IPPs from the 2002 power policy that sit in the government's renegotiation group.
